text: Lesson 11's worked example was the easy case — theta landed exactly on the grid. Real phases almost never do. This lesson is the honest version: what phase estimation actually returns when theta doesn't fit neatly into n bits, and what it costs to fix that.

With n counting qubits, outcomes land on an evenly spaced grid with spacing 1 over 2 to the n — that's the resolution, and it's structurally impossible to report anything finer, since only 2 to the n outcomes exist at all. Getting more resolution costs more than one extra qubit's worth of circuitry: going from n to n plus 1 qubits means the new top qubit must control U to the power of 2 to the n, so the largest power of U required doubles every single time you add one bit of precision. Ten bits needs U to the 512th; eleven bits needs U to the 1024th. Precision is cheap to ask for, and exponentially expensive to buy.

Here's the realistic case: theta equals 0.3, which can't be written exactly in any finite number of binary digits, with n equals 3 counting qubits, giving 8 possible outcomes. The verified probabilities show k equals 2, estimate 0.25, as the single most likely outcome at 57.75 percent — the nearest grid point to 0.3. But it's nowhere close to certain: k equals 3, the next-nearest point at 0.375, still gets 25.93 percent, and the remaining six outcomes soak up the rest. This spread is the honest signature of imprecision.

The standard way to tame that spread, from Nielsen and Chuang's treatment, is n equals m plus the ceiling of log base 2 of 2 plus 1 over 2 epsilon, to guarantee m bits of precision correct with probability at least 1 minus epsilon. The extra qubits beyond m don't add precision you report — they absorb exactly the kind of leakage shown in the theta equals 0.3 example, sharpening the peak around the nearest grid point and shrinking leakage into neighboring outcomes.
Next lesson shows this same four-step circuit reused, almost unchanged, inside Shor's algorithm, quantum chemistry simulation, and the HHL algorithm for linear systems.
